title: Industrial Hearing Protection: How to Pick the Right NRR for Your Plant Floor
summary: The press line is running, your foam earplugs are in, and a coworker is waving at you from two stations down. You pull one earplug out to hear what he's saying, and when you push it back in, it doesn't sit as deep as it did when you put it on this morning. By lunch, the earplug has worked itself loose without you noticing, and the press you stopped hearing hours ago is suddenly the loudest thing in the room. That's the difficulty with picking industrial hearing protection off a spec sheet. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on the package is a lab figure measured with a careful fit. OSHA's guidance subtracts 7 dB from that rating and, in some cases, cuts what's left in half. A hearing protector can look adequate on paper and still leave you over the limit, so choosing well means starting from your measured noise level and planning for fit, comfort, and the need to hear the people around you. Know Your Plant's Noise Exposure Before You Pick a Hearing Protector Before you compare a single hearing protector equipment, you have to find out how loud your area of the plant gets. Every method for judging a protector, from OSHA's to NIOSH's, starts from one number: your work area's noise level averaged over an 8-hour day. That figure is the time-weighted average (TWA). An NRR can't tell you anything useful until you know your TWA. OSHA's noise standard draws two lines. At an 85 dBA TWA, also called the action level, your employer has to run a hearing conservation program. At 90 dBA, the permissible exposure limit (PEL), hearing protection is required for all workers in that area. OSHA's rule also says your hearing protectors must bring your noise exposure level down to at least 90 dBA, and down to 85 dBA if your annual hearing test has already shown a significant drop in your hearing. That lower 85 dBA target is easy to overlook, and it raises the bar for anyone whose hearing has already slipped. For the full rule, including who has to provide protection and when, see our guide to OSHA hearing protection requirements. Noise levels vary a lot from one area of your plant to the next. Your own area's TWA comes from your employer's noise monitoring, which is part of a hearing conservation program. For a fuller chart of everyday and industrial sound levels, see our article on what dB level requires ear protection. Tip: If you don't know your area's TWA, ask your safety lead or supervisor. A phone app gives you a spot reading of one moment, and a TWA covers your whole workday. Once you know your number, the next decision is which hearing protector type you'll actually keep in for that whole workday. Industrial Earplugs, Earmuffs, and Earbuds Compared for the Plant Floor Your TWA tells you how much protection you need. The form factor of hearing protections decide how much of the labeled rating you get on an ordinary day at work, so it's worth comparing earplugs, earmuffs, and electronic earbuds side by side. Industrial Earplugs: High Lab Ratings, Wide Real-World Spread Foam earplugs carry some of the highest lab ratings on the shelf. Foam also shows the widest spread in real-world results, because the protection depends on how well you roll and insert each earplug. A shallow fit can cost you much of the rating, and a pre-molded earplug in the wrong size can leak in the same way. You can learn how to compare materials and sizes in our guide to choosing earplugs for work. Industrial Earmuffs: The Most Consistent Fit Earmuffs seal around your ear instead of inside it, so the fit varies less from one worker to the next. A supervisor can also see at a glance whether your industrial earmuffs are on. But earmuffs are the weakest option with thick safety glasses on your temples, a hot floor, and hard hats that aren't built to work with them. Electronic Earbuds and Earmuffs: Protection That Keeps Speech Audible Electronic hearing protection follows AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach. A microphone and circuit compresses loud machine noises to protect your ears while amplifying lower-level sounds like speech, backup alarms, and a machine changing pitch. On a long day, that awareness can decide whether your protection stays in or comes out. Electronic earbuds also add a slim fit that works with safety glasses. How the Three Types Compare on the Floor Each form factor trades protection, comfort, and awareness differently: Foam or pre-molded earplugs Passive earmuffs Electronic earbuds Electronic earmuffs Real-world consistency Lowest, depends on insertion High Depends on tip size and seal High With safety glasses No conflict Temples can break the seal No conflict Temples can break the seal On a hot floor Comfortable Cups can get hot Comfortable (check the IP rating) Cups can get hot Hearing coworkers Hard without removing them Hard without lifting a cup Hear-through keeps speech audible Hear-through keeps speech audible Easy for a supervisor to check No Yes No Yes Whichever type of hearing protection you choose, the NRR on its package overstates the protection you'll get on the floor. OSHA and NIOSH give you three ways to estimate by how much. Three Ways to Estimate Real-World Protection From an NRR Every hearing protector type mentioned above carries an NRR measured under the Environmental Protection Agency's labeling rule, with trained test subjects and a careful fit. Workers on a plant floor get less than that, so OSHA and NIOSH discount the label using three different methods. For more information on what the number measures, see our article on how NRR ratings work. Method One: OSHA's Appendix B Subtracts 7 dB From the NRR When your noise is measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B method tells you to subtract 7 dB from the NRR before you apply it. The 7 dB accounts for the difference between how the NRR is calculated and the A-weighted scale your noise meter reads. Estimated exposure = TWA − (NRR − 7) Method Two: OSHA's 50 Percent Safety Factor Gives a Conservative Planning Number OSHA compliance officers apply a further 50 percent safety factor to the NRR when they decide whether a plant should add engineering controls, which gives you (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. Under a hearing conservation program, OSHA judges your protector with the Appendix B number instead. For your own planning, the halved number becomes a sensible cushion for your measurements. The 50 percent factor leaves room for a rushed fit, a sweaty earmuff seal, and the gap your safety glasses create. Method Three: NIOSH Derates by Protector Type NIOSH recommends subtracting 25 percent of the labeled NRR for earmuffs, 50 percent for slow-recovery foam earplugs and 70 percent for all other earplugs, then applying the 7 dB correction for dBA measurements. The NIOSH method favors earmuffs and discounts most earplugs heavily, which reflects how each type tends to perform in the field. The Three Estimates Side by Side With AXIL Ratings Run AXIL's own ratings through all three methods and the spread is wide: Protector and area OSHA Appendix B (NRR − 7) OSHA 50 percent ((NRR − 7) ÷ 2) NIOSH (derated by type) MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 95 dBA 77 dBA 86 dBA 83 dBA MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 100 dBA 82 dBA 91 dBA (over the PEL) 88 dBA GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips, NRR 21, in 92 dBA 78 dBA 85 dBA About 88 dBA (foam earplug derate) The same earmuffs can look comfortably safe or over the limit depending on the method they’re measured with. So plan with the conservative number, then make sure your hearing protector is worn correctly, since a poor fit can cost you more protection than the difference between two products' ratings. A fit test goes one step past all three estimates. A fit test measures the protection on your own ears and gives you a Personal Attenuation Rating (PAR). If your hearing conservation program offers fit testing, a PAR is a better guide than any derated label. Derating tends to push buyers toward the highest NRR on the shelf. On a floor at the lower end of the noise range, though, too much protection creates a different hazard. Hearing Overprotection Can Mute Alarms and Speech Hearing overprotection can mute the sounds that keep you safe on the work floor, like a forklift horn, a backup alarm, or a coworker's warning. A worker who can't hear those sounds faces a different kind of injury risk. Overprotection can also lead you to lift an earmuff or pull an earplug every time you need to talk, which removes your hearing protection while the noise is still there. NIOSH advises against overprotection and suggests aiming for just enough reduction to bring your exposure to roughly 75 to 85 dBA. The UK's Health and Safety Executive recommends avoiding protectors that bring the level at your ear below 70 dB. A worked example shows how easy it is to overshoot. Take a foam earplug rated NRR 33 in an 88 dBA area. OSHA's Appendix B method puts your exposure at 88 − 26 = 62 dBA, well below both targets. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21) in that same area land at 74 dBA with Appendix B and 81 dBA with the 50 percent factor, close to or inside NIOSH's range either way. Electronic hear-through also helps at this end of the range. Hear-through lets you choose a moderate NRR and still amplify the sound of alarms and speech that a passive protector would mute. You can learn more in our guide to how electronic hearing protection works. At the top of the noise range, the risk runs the other way. Above 100 dBA, a single protector of any type can leave you short. When to Double Up: Dual Protection Above 100 dBA Double up when your 8-hour TWA tops 100 dBA, the point where NIOSH recommends wearing earplugs and earmuffs together. The 91 dBA result for MX Passive earmuffs in a 100 dBA area shows why a single protector runs out of room there. OSHA's general industry standard doesn't require dual protection. In mining, MSHA requires both an earplug and an earmuff once a miner's TWA exceeds 105 dBA. To estimate your combined protection, the OSHA Technical Manual takes the field-adjusted rating of the higher-rated protector and adds 5 dB. Never add the two NRRs together, because two layers block far less than the sum of their ratings. Here's how much protection doubling up adds for MX Passive earmuffs (NRR 25) worn over GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21): Field-adjusted MX Passive rating: (25 − 7) ÷ 2 = 9 dB Add 5 dB for the second layer: 9 + 5 = 14 dB Estimated exposure in a 100 dBA area: 100 − 14 = 86 dBA, back under the PEL In a 105 dBA area, the same pairing estimates 91 dBA. If your work area runs that loud, talk to your safety lead about engineering controls alongside hearing protection equipment. Dual protection only works if you can tolerate both layers for the whole work day. Slim earbuds under an earmuff cushion can feel more comfortable over a long day than bulky foam earplugs under the same earmuffs. Our guide to doubling up with plugs and muffs covers how to wear both layers so each one seals. Two layers also make it harder to hear the people around you, and hearing your coworkers is often the reason protection comes out in the middle of the work day. Industrial Earbuds Let You Hear Coworkers While Protecting Your Hearing On a loud floor, hearing protection often gets pulled off because you need to talk, catch an instruction, or answer a call. NIOSH reports that 28 percent of noise-exposed manufacturing workers say they don't wear hearing protection precisely because they need to hear other sounds during the workday. Hear-Through Keeps Speech and Alarms Audible in Your Earbuds Electronic industrial earbuds let you keep your hearing protection in while you talk. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds compress sounds above 85 dB and amplify lower-level sounds, like a coworker's voice or a backup alarm, up to 5X. That's AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach on the work floor, and it means the coworker waving at you from two stations down no longer means you have to take an earplug out of your ear. Industrial earbuds handle that need differently from the other three ways workers stay in contact on a floor: Passive protection and raised voices. You'll end up shouting, or lifting your ear protection to hear. Electronic earmuffs. Electronic earmuffs give you the same hear-through, but safety glasses at your temples can break the earmuff seal over a long day. Radio-integrated headsets. A two-way radio is built into the earmuff itself, which suits crews that run everything over the radio. Bluetooth Earbuds Handle Calls Within Plant Rules Bluetooth calling suits supervisors and maintenance staff who move between areas and need to use their phones without removing their hearing protection. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds limit Bluetooth volume while the hearing enhancement stays on, which keeps a call or music volume at a safer level. Every plant sets its own audio policy, so confirm yours before you rely on Bluetooth. Consumer Noise-Cancelling Earbuds Fall Short of Industrial Protection Consumer noise-cancelling earbuds can look a lot like industrial earbuds, but they belong in a separate category. OSHA says most consumer active noise-cancelling headphones aren't effective for controlling occupational noise, and recommends against using them in place of laboratory-tested protectors . Our article on why noise cancelling is not hearing protection explains the difference. Hearing your coworkers keeps your hearing protection in place, and so does a hearing protector gear that stays comfortable for a 10- or 12-hour day. Comfort, Fit and PPE Compatibility on Long Workdays A Good Seal Has to Hold Up for 10 or 12 Hours Over a long workday, small fit problems add up as your earplugs work loose and your earmuff cushions become warm and soften against your ears. Fit can have a bigger effect on your hearing protection than most spec-sheet differences. The difference between a well-inserted and a poorly inserted earplug can be larger than the difference between two products' NRRs. Tip: With hear-through switched off on your hearing protection, say a few words out loud. Your voice should sound deeper and fuller inside your head when your foam tips are sealed in your ears. If your voice sounds thin, go up a size in your ear tips and reseat them. The tips that come with your hearing protection gear are pre-installed are only a default, so using a different size in each ear is normal. Safety Glasses, Heat and Hard Hats Test Your Seal All Day Safety glasses can break your earmuff’s seal. Each temple arm lifts the earmuff cushion off your skin and lets noise leak in. Thin, flat safety glasses arms at your temples leave the smallest gap, and in-ear protection avoids this problem altogether because there's no cushion for your glasses to lift. On a hot floor, sweat and water resistance are also worth checking on your hearing protection gear. The GS Extreme 3.0, XCOR PRO, and MXII Pro each carry an IP65 rating. AXIL's MX earmuffs use an over-the-head headband. If you wear a hard hat, confirm your hearing protection’s fit with your specific hard hat before spending a full day on the work floor, or pair your hard hat with in-ear protection instead. Battery Life Has to Cover Your Whole Workday Electronic protection only enhances what you hear while the battery lasts. AXIL products have varying runtimes depending on the mode you use: Product Hear-through only Bluetooth only Hear-through plus Bluetooth GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds Up to 40 hours Up to 20 hours Up to 15 hours XCOR PRO earbuds Up to 13 hours Up to 7 hours Up to 5 hours MXII Pro earmuffs About 60 hours About 45 hours About 40 hours MX Pro earmuffs 70 hours 40 hours 30 hours You Can Ask for a Protector That Fits If the hearing protector your plant issues doesn't work for you, say so. OSHA requires employers to let you choose from a variety of suitable hearing protectors, so you're entitled to pick one that fits. AXIL's industrial lineup divides along those same lines: noise level, in-ear or over-ear, and how much hear-through and runtime you need. Matching AXIL Hearing Protection to Plant Floor Noise Levels Matching a hearing protector to your noise level works best with a cautious number. Every estimate here uses OSHA's conservative 50 percent method, so a well-fitted protector should perform better than the figure shown. If your hearing tests have already recorded a drop in your hearing, plan against the 85 dBA target and consider doubling up your hearing protection starting at about 95 dBA. The GS Extreme 3.0 runs up to 15 hours with Bluetooth and hear-through combined. Best for: 85 to 90 dBA areas, safety-glasses wearers and long days on a hot floor. XCOR PRO Earbuds XCOR PRO earbuds carry an NRR of 21 to 23 depending on the ear tip, plus 85 dB digital compression and hearing enhancement. XCOR PRO earbuds run up to 5 hours with Bluetooth and hear-through combined, so plan a charge on your break during a 10- or 12-hour day. Best for: in-ear protection close to the 90 dBA line. MX Electronic, MX Pro and MXII Pro Earmuffs AXIL's electronic earmuffs carry NRRs of 22 to 23 and amplify ambient sound while compressing loud noise. MX Pro adds Bluetooth, and MXII Pro adds Bluetooth, IP65 resistance and about 60 hours of hear-through runtime. MX Electronic covers the same hear-through job without Bluetooth. Best for: 90 to 95 dBA areas where you need to hear coworkers and want hearing protection your supervisor can check at a glance. MX Passive Earmuffs MX Passive earmuffs carry an NRR of 25 with no electronics or batteries to manage. MX Passive earmuffs also work as the outer layer when you double up with earbuds. Best for: 95 to 99 dBA areas, and dual protection above 100 dBA. Industrial Hearing Protection FAQs What is the best hearing protection for industrial work? The best industrial hearing protection is the protector that clears your measured exposure after derating and that you'll keep in for your whole workday. As a rough guide, electronic earbuds suit 85 to 90 dBA, electronic or passive earmuffs suit 90 to 99 dBA, and earplugs or earbuds under earmuffs suit areas above 100 dBA. What are the best ear muffs for industrial use? Look for earmuffs that still clear your exposure after NIOSH's 25 percent derate, seal well with your safety glasses, fit with your hard hat and stay comfortable in heat. You can compare options in AXIL's earmuffs collection. How do you calculate NRR for OSHA? For noise measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B subtracts 7 dB from the NRR: TWA − (NRR − 7). For a conservative field estimate, halve the adjusted rating: (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. An NRR 25 earmuff in 95 dBA gives 77 dBA with Appendix B and 86 dBA with the 50 percent factor. Electronic industrial earbuds let you keep your hearing protection in while you talk.[GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0) compress sounds above 85 dB and amplify lower-level sounds, like a coworker's voice or a backup alarm, up to 5X. That's AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach on the work floor, and it means the coworker waving at you from two stations down no longer means you have to take an earplug out of your ear.


Industrial earbuds handle that need differently from the other three ways workers stay in contact on a floor:


1. Passive protection and raised voices. You'll end up shouting, or lifting your ear protection to hear.
2. Electronic earmuffs. Electronic earmuffs give you the same hear-through, but safety glasses at your temples can break the earmuff seal over a long day.
3. Radio-integrated headsets. A two-way radio is built into the earmuff itself, which suits crews that run everything over the radio.


### Bluetooth Earbuds Handle Calls Within Plant Rules


Bluetooth calling suits supervisors and maintenance staff who move between areas and need to use their phones without removing their hearing protection.[GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0) limit Bluetooth volume while the hearing enhancement stays on, which keeps a call or music volume at a safer level. Every plant sets its own audio policy, so confirm yours before you rely on Bluetooth.


### Consumer Noise-Cancelling Earbuds Fall Short of Industrial Protection


Consumer noise-cancelling earbuds can look a lot like industrial earbuds, but they belong in a separate category. OSHA says[most consumer active noise-cancelling headphones aren't effective for controlling occupational noise](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2023-03-06) , and recommends against using them in place of laboratory-tested protectors . Our[article on why noise cancelling is not hearing protection](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/cancellation-vs-protection) explains the difference.


Hearing your coworkers keeps your hearing protection in place, and so does a hearing protector gear that stays comfortable for a 10- or 12-hour day.


## Comfort, Fit and PPE Compatibility on Long Workdays


### A Good Seal Has to Hold Up for 10 or 12 Hours


Over a long workday, small fit problems add up as your earplugs work loose and your earmuff cushions become warm and soften against your ears. Fit can have a bigger effect on your hearing protection than most spec-sheet differences. The difference between a well-inserted and a poorly inserted earplug can be larger than the difference between two products' NRRs.


**Tip:** With hear-through switched off on your hearing protection, say a few words out loud. Your voice should sound deeper and fuller inside your head when your foam tips are sealed in your ears. If your voice sounds thin, go up a size in your ear tips and reseat them. The tips that come with your hearing protection gear are pre-installed are only a default, so using a different size in each ear is normal.


### Safety Glasses, Heat and Hard Hats Test Your Seal All Day


Safety glasses can break your earmuff’s seal. Each temple arm lifts the earmuff cushion off your skin and lets noise leak in. Thin, flat safety glasses arms at your temples leave the smallest gap, and in-ear protection avoids this problem altogether because there's no cushion for your glasses to lift.


On a hot floor, sweat and water resistance are also worth checking on your hearing protection gear. The[GS Extreme 3.0](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0) ,[XCOR PRO](https://goaxil.com/products/xcor) , and[MXII Pro](https://goaxil.com/products/mxii-pro) each carry an IP65 rating.

## Industrial Hearing Protection FAQs


What is the best hearing protection for industrial work?


The best industrial hearing protection is the protector that clears your measured exposure after derating and that you'll keep in for your whole workday. As a rough guide, electronic earbuds suit 85 to 90 dBA, electronic or passive earmuffs suit 90 to 99 dBA, and earplugs or earbuds under earmuffs suit areas above 100 dBA.


What are the best ear muffs for industrial use?


Look for earmuffs that still clear your exposure after NIOSH's 25 percent derate, seal well with your safety glasses, fit with your hard hat and stay comfortable in heat. You can compare options in AXIL's earmuffs collection.


How do you calculate NRR for OSHA?


For noise measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B subtracts 7 dB from the NRR: TWA − (NRR − 7). For a conservative field estimate, halve the adjusted rating: (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. An NRR 25 earmuff in 95 dBA gives 77 dBA with Appendix B and 86 dBA with the 50 percent factor.


When is double hearing protection needed in a factory?


NIOSH recommends earplugs plus earmuffs once your TWA tops 100 dBA. To estimate combined protection, add 5 dB to the field-adjusted rating of the higher-rated protector.


Can hearing protection be too strong?


Yes. Protection that brings the level at your ear below about 70 dB can mask alarms, machine sounds and speech. NIOSH suggests aiming for roughly 75 to 85 dBA.


Does "industrial grade" mean anything on hearing protection?


No standard defines "industrial grade." Look for an NRR label, which the EPA requires on hearing protectors sold in the US, and for the ANSI test report behind that label.


Are Bluetooth earbuds allowed on a factory floor?


OSHA doesn't ban Bluetooth earbuds, and many employers set their own limits on audio near moving equipment. Check your plant's policy, and choose earbuds with a tested NRR instead of consumer earbuds.


What does OSHA require for hearing protection?


OSHA requires employers to provide hearing protectors at an 85 dBA TWA and to make sure protection brings exposure to 90 dBA or below, or 85 dBA for workers whose hearing tests show a significant drop. Our OSHA hearing protection requirements guide covers the full rule.


## Your First Steps to the Right Industrial Hearing Protection


Your measured noise level at your work area drives every choice you make about your hearing protection. A good seal in your hearing protection gear decides how much noise reaches your ear. Run these steps to ensure your ears get the best protection:


1. Ask your safety lead or supervisor for your area's TWA.
2. Run that TWA through OSHA's 50 percent method and aim for a result between roughly 75 and 85 dBA, which guards against hearing underprotection and overprotection at the same time.
3. Pick the form factor that suits your safety glasses, your hard hat, and how often you need to hear coworkers.
4. During your first week, check your seal at the start of the day and after every break, since those are the moments your hearing protection’s fit tends to slip.
5. Ask for a fit test and a PAR if your plant offers one, and recheck your choice whenever your work area's noise changes, like if you get a new press, a new line, or need to move to a different station.
